Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 18, to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to move the second reading of this bill I desire to give to the house the information which I promised three different members would be forthcoming on the motion for second reading. The information is with regard to the area affected by drought in the three western provinces, the general conditions which have existed in that section of Canada since it was first settled, the actions which have been taken by different governments which have been in power from time to time to deal with the situation, and the details of what is intended to be done during the coming year under the present legislation.
I think I can best outline the area which has been affected by referring to the map which I have in my hand. If you take a point on the boundary line between Canada and the United States immediately south of the town of Morden in Manitoba and draw a line directly from there to the town of Lloyd-minster, which is located on the boundary line between Alberta and Saskatchewan, just south of where the North Saskatchewan river enters the province of Saskatchewan, then westward and southward to about the town of Cochrane, west of Calgary, and then directly south to where the western boundary of Alberta meets the American boundary line, generally
768	COMMONS
Farm Rehabilitation-Mr. Gardiner
speaking you will have taken in the area known as the open prairie country of western Canada which has been affected by what we have been pleased to call the drought in recent years.
Could the minister give the number of acres in that area?

I think I can give all that information in a general way. Before going on to discuss the general question, I should like to make this general statement which I am sure will meet with the approval of everyone who has been interested in the problem. I believe the great majority of the people in that area, while realizing that they have suffered manj- hardships, would wish me to emphasize the fact that they appreciate the efforts which have been put forth by the Red Cross, by governing bodies generally, by the railways, by individuals and communities in other parts of Canada, and by creditors in general to make their burden lighter during this period of difficulty which has extended for from five to seven years. I think the great majority, if not all, of the people in that vast area believe that a real effort has been made, by all those to whom I have referred, to do something to lighten the burden of those who are passing through these difficulties.
I might describe in another way the area that is affected. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said the day before yesterday, about three hundred municipalities are affected. I would estimate that the acreage contained in those three hundred municipalities would be approximately 60,000,000. Of course that 60,000,000 acres embraces all the different types of land that are to be found within the area I defined a moment ago, and includes not only the land but the portion of it which may be covered by water. The whole area, figured out on an acreage basis-640 acres to the square mile -covers a little over 60,000,000 acres. I think I should be well w'ithin the mark if I were to say that about 45.000,000 acres, or about three fourths, of that land is occupied, but probably not more than about 20,000,000 acres of it has been improved. In other words, not more than about 20,000.000 acres in that area have actually been used for the production of crops, and the raising of live stock, as we understand the term when we speak of small farmers having stock running on pasture. That would cover the area that has been affected more or less during the last six or seven years.

The only qualification I would make in the description of the area would be that as you follow that long line from south of Morden on to Lloydminster, and that long line from Lloydminster down to Cochrane, zig-zagging back and forth across it you will find differing conditions. Sometimes you will find the land north of the line affected by drought, and in other cases you can go well into the southern section and find land which has not been affected by drought for any considerable number of years.
I might add that you have within that area, well within the centre of it in some cases, sections of territory which have not felt the real effect of the drought in the same way that other sections of the territory have. For example, you can take the heavy lands fhat surround Regina city and Moose Jaw. Those lands, while well within that area, have not been affected to the same extent as lands farther south and farther west that are not as heavy in their texture. Then we have right in the centre of the larger district. about the town of Rosetown, and to the south of Rosetown on towards Elrose, a section of country w'hich during t.he whole period of the drought and the difficulties of the drought have had a fair crop. In some years it has been better than in others, but in any case these people during the greater part of the time have been able to keep entirely off relief. The same is true of the majority of people who live on the heavy lands around the city of Regina and the city of Moose Jaw.
I would point out that this year the area does not take in quite the 300 municipalities, but it does take in a larger area than it has in any one of the previous seven years. This year the area affected, which has been admitted to the care and administration of the federal government so far as assistance is concerned, covers about 250 municipalities. This area represents more than 50,000,000 acres of land, about 35,000,000 acres of which is occupied, and about 18,000,000 acres of which is improved or being farmed in the ordinary sense of the term.

About 18,000,000 of the
35.000.	000, yes. I think the size of this area can be better appreciated if I put it in this way. The area comprises more than one-quarter of the occupied, and more than one-fifth of the improved, area of farm land in the whole Dominion of Canada. I do not know whether that is generally understood or not. but I repeat that the occupied part of

Farm Rehabilitation-Mr. Gardiner
what is now generally called throughout Canada the drought area, but which I prefer to call the open prairie section of western Canada, has within it one-quarter of all the occupied farm land in the Dominion of Canada and a little more than one-fifth of the improved farm land in the Dominion of Canada. I might say further that it contains a population of approximately 900,000 people-almost equal to the entire population of the province of Saskatchewan. It is a population greater than that of any province in the Dominion of Canada except the two great central provinces of Quebec and Ontario. That I think expresses more completely the importance of the problem from the p'feint of view of the Dominion of Canada than any mere statement of what the area is and the acreage involved. The population affected is equal to that of the third greatest province in Canada in point of population, and greater than the population of any other province except the two largest provinces in the dominion.
Within that area, inside the lines I have spoken of, you have the city of Calgary, the city of Lethbridge, and the city of Medicine Hat in the province of Alberta; you have the cities of Moose Jaw, Weyburn, Swift Current, Regina, Saskatoon and North Battle-ford in the province of Saskatchewan. I recite these facts, Mr. Speaker, in order to impress upon the house, if I can, the impossibility of even considering the question of placing such a large number as 900,000 people to better advantage in any other part of the dominion.
Does that 900,000 include the cities and towns?

Yes, it includes the cities and towns, which are largely dependent on the area in which they are located.
I think I have said sufficient, Mr. Speaker, to impress upon the house the importance of the question that has to be dealt with under any legislation having to do with rehabilitation, and as well the importance of that area to the remaining part of Canada.
There has been a great deal of discussion during the last seven or eight years as to whether difficulties of this kind were experienced in the prairie sections of Canada prior to the last five or six years, whether the lands in that area have been depleted by winds and other conditions, whether they have been depleted by certain methods of farming. All these questions naturally arise in our minds as a result of the experience we have been having in the last six or seven years. I make bold to say that if we had any other kind of climate than what we have in the
prairie provinces, people could not live there and maintain homes. I think that statement can be made without fear of contradiction. If we had any different kind of climate in the area I have described, people could not live there if they relied upon farming for their maintenance. I should like to take a moment or two to give my reasons for making this statement.
In the first place the western plains of Canada are divided into three steppes, and the borders of those steppes of prairie and park land run parallel with the Rocky mountains. These borders in the form of hills run from the northwest down towards the southeast. The first steppe, the one nearest the Rockies, extends from the foothills to the	east of	the mountains	just tothe west of	the city	of Moose	Jaw	and itseastern border almost parallels the Rocky mountains. The edge of the next steppe runs just east of the city of Brandon, and again parallels the Rocky mountains, w-hile the edge of the third	steppe	parallels	the	Rockiesthrough a point east of Winnipeg. The area contained in the third steppe averages about 800 feet above sea level. The area contained in the second steppe, which extends from Brandon to	Moose	Jaw, has	an	average
height of about 1,600 feet above sea level, while the area contained in the steppe extending from Moose Jaw to the foothills of the Rocky mountains has an average altitude of about 3,400 feet above sea level.
Those who are familiar with the western part of Canada know that the growth in the first steppe is naturally different from the growth in the second steppe, while the growth in the third steppe, is different from either of the other two. You find oaks and elms, similar to those in eastern Canada, growing in the Red river valley. You find poplars and willows growing in the second steppe, but the natural growth in the third steppe, at least in the southern part of it, is short grass, and for that reason we speak of it as prairie country.
One of the reasons why I say it would be very difficult if not almost impossible for people to live in that area under any other climate is shown by the figures of average rainfall which I should like to present:

These are the centres of some of the most important farming areas in Canada, stretching right from the Pacific to the Atlantic. Hon. members will note that as compared with any other part of Canada the rainfall in those prairie sections is very much less. Someone may say that Vancouver is almost as far north as Lethbridge and Regina, so why is it that crops cannot be grown with equal success on the other side of the mountains. That reason is found in the fact that the Rocky mountains lie between Vancouver and the prairies, and the winds that come over the warm currents of the Pacific ocean carry both moisture and heat, giving a more equable temperature during the year on the western side of the Rocky mountains. When they cross over to the eastern side of the mountains they are associated with temperatures ranging from 110 degrees above zero, as we had it last July, to 40 and SO degrees below zero, as we have it in January. Then you have the seasons shortened by the fact that the warm winds do not come over the mountains, and therefore, since we are so far north and at such an altitude above sea level, it would be impossible to produce farm crops if we had as much rain as they have in Vancouver. Perhaps that may be understood better if I remind hon. members that any year we get more than the average rainfall on the western prairies we are afraid of one of two things. We are afraid of rust which we had in 1934, or we are afraid of frost, which we had in 1907. Of course we have had frost in many other years that I could enumerate, but 1907 was most severe.
I recite these facts in order to indicate that those plains are particularly suited to the production of certain crops because of the climatic conditions that exist. In recent days there has been some controversy as to the possibilities of the Peace River country for the production of wheat, as compared with the open prairie country. I am not going to enter into that controversy in any way. The Peace River country is suited to the growing of some varieties of wheat. The northeastern part of the province of Saskatchewan is suited to the growing of some varieties of wheat. The province of Manitoba is suited to the growing of certain varieties of wheat. But the one section of western Canada which, under all conditions excepting those of frost, extreme drought or too great rainfall at certain seasons of the year, is certain to produce No. 1 Northern wheat or in some instances No. 1 hard wheat, is the short grass prairie region of western Canada. No. 1 Northern wheat or No. 1 hard wheat are known the world over as

strong wheat, and there is no other place in the world where a better variety of strong, hard spring wheat can be grown than in those short grass prairie regions. One of the reasons for that is that you can grow hard wheat only where you have a comparatively low rainfall and at the same time fairly long and fairly cool nights. These are the two conditions that contribute to the high protein content wheat that is being produced in those areas.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I repeat that I make bold to say that if you had any other kind of climate in that part of western Canada it would be impossible to maintain a population there at all, doing what we are attempting to do at the present time. I should like to ask this question: What does the history of the area show? Well, I do not know whether you call it good fortune or bad, but I have always considered it good; I have had the privilege of living in the prairie sections of North America ever since 1890, with the exception of the four years from 1896 to 1900. During five years of that time, from 1890 to 1895, I lived in the state of Nebraska, which is in the heart of that part of the United States that has suffered so severely within the last few years. What I want to say to the house is this, that during the period through which we are passing we have not experienced anything more difficult than farmers all through the prairie section of the central part of the United States experienced during the nineties of the last century. The area of Canada of which I am now speaking was not settled in the sense that it is settled to-day, but from the old timers who live in it I understand that exactly the same climatic conditions prevailed over that area in the nineties as have prevailed during the last five or six years.
Most of us in this house can remember the experiences of the years from 1914 to 1921. I have brought to the house the records of crop yields during some of the years since this section of country has been settled, and I have done so in order that I might more fully illustrate to you what I have in mind in the statements I have just made. Let us take crop district No. 3. This district lies between the Soo line in Saskatchewan and Shaunavon- or rather it extends almost to Shaunavon. It runs up on the north of Swift Current towards the Saskatchewan river, taking a triangle out of the centre of the southern part of the province. I find that in 1914 the farmers in that district harvested a little under two bushels to the acre on all the land then under cultivation. That is a poorer crop than they have had in district No. 3 in any year since 1914;

It has to do with the history of this particular area-and when I speak of the history of it I mean the settling of that particular part of the country. It is in this matter that I think some obligation rests upon the people of all Canada in connection with that area. Prior to 1905 this area was comprised in the Northwest Territories and administered by a government situated at Regina. But that government did not have the same powers, particularly in connection with finance, as the provincial governments which later were set up. The immigration policy in connection with the settlement of that area was administered entirely from Ottawa. The western areas differed in some degree from other parts of Canada in regard to settlement. The lands and resources of the eastern provinces and of British Columbia were owned and controlled by the provinces, and they had some control of the settlement of such lands. When the western part of Canada was first being opened up one or two things were done that seemed wise at the time but the wisdom of which, reviewed in the light of experience of this district of which I am now speaking, has turned out to be at least questionable. One of these had to do with the system of survey that was adopted. If I understand rightly, we copied that system from the United States. The country was blocked off into areas twenty-four miles square; then these were divided into four parts six miles square, and those again split into sections; then people were brought in and settled on quarter sections, cut out here and there all over the country. In such areas as the heavy lands around the city of Regina, those around Rosetown, and some of the heavy land areas in Manitoba, that system worked out successfully and settlement was carried on in a way well suited to those sections. If I remember aright, when that bill was introduced in the house the statement was made that while a farmer could make a good living on a quarter-section of land in the settled areas of western Canada, it would not be possible for him to do so in the areas we are discussing this afternoon; therefore the position was taken that men going into that section to homestead should be given a quarter-section of land free of any other charge than the S10 homesteading fee and the three years' residence requirement, and also the right, if desired, to purchase another quarter-section at $3 per acre. I shall be able to give the exact figures when the estimate comes down, and perhaps it would be better not to attempt to speak accurately until then; but I can say that a considerable number of these dugouts and dams have been completed over the whole area.
We have deemed it advisable to set up a central office in Regina and there we are compiling all the information that is available from the municipal authorities and the provincial and dominion governments with regard to moisture condition, soil condition and so forth in these areas; and in addition to that we are completing a survey made in the province down to the first of January, 1935, showing ownership of lands in the area. We hope to have that survey completed early this spring, and, when it is, we intend to call into conference representatives of all the organizations mentioned in the original act and there determine upon some line of policy to deal with the situation. To indicate what I have in mind, I may say this. There is an area where a complete survey has been made in the northwestern part of Saskatchewan. There is another in Alberta. The area in Saskatchewan shows that in a considerable extent of country there are only fourteen farmers still left on the land, because these lands are marginal lands. In all probability the fourteen who are there are among the best of the farmers who were in the district to begin with, and they are still there partly because they have a run for their cattle near where they are living. What we hope to do is to get the cooperation of the railway companies, which still have an interest in some of these lands; the cooperation of mortgage companies, who may have some interest; the cooperation of municipalities who may have taken over lands for unpaid taxes, and the cooperation of the provincial and federal governments, in getting the people moved off, say from a piece of mortgage company land in the centre of the area to a piece of land owned by the mortgage company outside the area, transferring the obligation along with the farmer. Then we hope to be able to have the whole marginal area fenced and turned into what may be called a community pasture. In other words, instead of trying to convince the people of that section that the land should

all be turned back to range country, comparatively small areas, which are surrounded by better land, should be selected and turned into community pastures, which should be placed at the disposal of the people in the neighbourhood without cost to the individual other than the fees he pays to put his stock there. And yet, looking down over the bank of a ravine such as that of the Qu'Appelle, if he is far enough north, or the Frenchman river, if he is in the southwestern corner, or the valley of the Saskatchewan, spots of land can be seen upon which he could live and use the land to much better advantage than it is now being used if there were means of getting there. Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) upon the statement he has made. While there are many matters that we do not view in exactly the same light, I doubt whether I have ever heard the case for the farmers in the drought area of western Canada presented in a more informative or comprehensive manner. The constituency to which I belong is in the centre of the drought area, and therefore I feel that in discussing this problem I am not asking the house to devote its attention to a merely local problem. This problem affects more than half the province of Saskatchewan as well as large areas in Manitoba and Alberta. The problem of drought affects the welfare of hundreds of thousands of people in western Canada and ultimately the welfare of the entire dominion. The problems of the drought area may be divided mainly into two classifications.

First, there are the problems directly attributable to economic conditions. In common with the rest of Canada we have felt the repercussions of the world^wide depression which has been in effect since the fall of 1929. I am cognizant of the fact that every section of Canada has its own peculiar economic problem, and western Canada is no exception. However, there are several particular problems that have led to straitened economic circumstances in the west, and it is my intention to review these briefly.
The present economic condition of the prairie provinces had its origin in part, as the minister has already said, in certain mistakes in early land settlement policies. These were evolved and applied at a time when the control of the natural resources of the province was administered from Ottawa. It is unnecessary for our purposes here to endeavour to place the blame for these mistakes; suffice it to say that some 290,000 farm families were scattered over a huge triangle, the longer side of which stretched for some 1,200 miles from southeastern Manitoba to the Peace River block in British Columbia. Hindsight is always better than foresight, and it is apparent now that some more orderly type of farm settlement would have saved enormous sums of money during the past forty years. If outer areas had been opened up, only after reasonably close settlement along a limited network of railway mileage, the population would have been better supplied with roads, schools and transportation services at a much lower cost.
Another mistake made was throwing open for settlement large areas of sub-marginal lands, unsuitable in many respects for the growing of grain. Even under the best possible conditions, only a precarious livelihood could be hoped for in such areas, and in times of drought only failure could be expected. No continuous or extensive attempt was made to test the soil scientifically or to determine the sources and amount of water available. Where attempts were made to classify new land, these were ignored totally by the incoming settlers.
Added to the mistakes made in land settlement is the even more serious problem of the burden of debts now being carried by the people of the prairie provinces. Under the urge of speculation, farm and other properties were bought for sums out of all proportion to their capacity to produce. On the strength of prices prevailing at that time, money was borrowed against these newly acquired lands at high rates of interest. It is useless to say that the debtors were not compelled to

borrow, for it can be said just as truthfully that the creditors did not have to lend. The money was not lent to the western pioneer because of any philanthropic motives. Money was lent to the west because higher rates of interest were available there than could be secured in the east. Money was invested in western Canada for purely business reasons; it was a partnership in which both parties hoped to profit. What was true of agriculture and business was equally true of municipal and provincial bodies. Expanding prosperity seemed to warrant heavy capital expenditures. In those days there were to be found lenders just as eager to lend as the borrowers were to borrow.
It is unnecessary to review in any detail the results which followed the deflationary period, commonly referred to as the depression. With the sudden falling of prices of all primary commodities, there occurred conversely an increase in the value of the dollar. Debts that had been incurred when wheat was $2 per bushel had to be met with wheat selling at fifty cents or less per bushel. The value of property dropped alarmingly and was no longer considered as good security. Loans were called in and credit restricted. As a result, farmers, workers and businessmen are now faced with the problem of debts, the principal of which cannot be paid at existing prices and to which has been added, in most cases, the unpaid interest for the past five or six years.
The Minister of Agriculture made some reference to the attempts which have been made along the lines of debt adjustment and to the debts which have been cancelled during the past year. I have no wish to digress from the matter before the house and get into the question of debt adjustment, but I should like to point out that the problem facing the western farmer who has had to accept debt adjustment can be summed up in a single paragraph contained in the standard renewal agreement which these farmers have been compelled to sign. I quote as follows:
For better securing the punctual payment of the moneys payable under these presents and said mortgage, and pursuant to the Land Titles Act, the farmer does hereby agree to become and does become tenant to the mortgagee of the said land, and the mortgagee does hereby lease the said land to the farmer for a term of three years from the 1st day of January, 1937, at a yearly rental of one-third of the whole crop of grain of the different kinds and qualities grown on the said land in each year, to become due and payable at the time of cutting of any of the said crop. The mortgagee may at any time after default under these presents determine the said tenancy without any notice to quit.

Nor have government bodies fared any better. Municipal and provincial authorities have been called upon to assume hitherto undreamed of responsibilities in the way of relief. Feed and seed requirements had to be met, and added to these was the fact that revenues were curtailed because of the inability of large numbers of the population to pay their taxes. It has been estimated that the funded debt of the three prairie provinces is in excess of $500,000,000, and that the net municipal debts, including those of municipally owned utilities, are in excess of $300,000,000. There must be added to these amounts the huge sum owing in farm and urban mortgages, balances due on agreements of sale and on commercial accounts. When we add to all this the freight discrimination which has operated for years against western Canada; when we consider further the fact-this is taken from the report of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) as published in 1934-that the tariff cost the western provinces $54,925,352 in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1931, and when we recall to mind the fact that, with the exception of the years mentioned by the minister, the price of wheat has seldom equaled the cost of production, it must be clear to hon. members why the economic conditions of western Canada are so acute.
As I said, there is a second classification of conditions affecting the welfare of the people of western Canada. I refer now, not to the economic conditions which are general throughout Canada, but to the climatic conditions which are peculiar to the section known as the drought area. For the past five years drought has affected an area of 75,000 square miles, including some of the best wheat land on the North American continent. This area is on a front of about 700 miles in length. When we call to mind that in 1928 one billion bushels-let there be no mistake, one thousand million bushels-of grain were produced in western Canada, and when we realize that over much of that land black blizzards have since blown with relentless fury, we can understand how parts of that country have been reduced to a veritable desert.
The real tragedy of the drought, however, was not the loss of crops, but the fact that the absence of water meant the loss of hogs, cattle, poultry and vegetable gardens. In short, the drought took from the prairie dweller his livelihood and left him, for the first time in his experience, entirely dependent upon the outside for his daily food. The result has been a lower standard of living for western people. Relief measures may have provided sufficient to keep body and soul
together, but there has been no way of replenishing the stock of dishes, bedding and furniture that have worn out during the period of the drought. The vitality of our people has been slowly sapped; their health has suffered; the social life of the drought area population has been seriously impaired, with disastrous results to the mental and physical condition of our people. The Wey-burn Mental Hospital, located in the constituency which I represent, is at the present time admitting an average of over one person per day to that institution. Education has been maintained only because some of our teachers with undaunted courage have continued to teach in rural schools for the unheard of pittance of from one to three hundred dollars a year.

Nor has the drought problem affected the rural population alone. The greatly diminished purchasing power of the farmers in the drought area has meant hardship for the workers, professional and business men whose livelihood depends upon the farmers' prosperity. Merchants and professional men have found it impossible to collect back debts and have been compelled in many instances to continue serving the drought-stricken farmer without any hope of immediate remuneration. Workers have found that lower wages and unemployment have inevitably followed the bankruptcy of the western farmer.
The effect of this combination of economic and climatic conditions has been twofold. First, it has produced a system of relief of the most pernicious kind. Since the opening

Farm Rehabilitation-Mr. Douglas
of the session some statements have been made in this house with reference to racketeering in the matter of relief. May I ask the house why we have such a condition? Is it not largely that we have placed a premium upon improvidence? In Saskatchewan, for instance, the government has a relief schedule depending upon the number of persons in the family, but there are deductions if the farmer milks cows, keeps chickens or raises hogs, with the result that the farmer is best off who does the least to help himself.
The second effect has been on one of our greatest natural resources, namely, the wheat growing land of western Canada, which is in danger of being very rapidly wiped out. The report of the Canadian Conservation Institute shows that the area affected by drought is slowly spreading northward, and unless some immediate steps are taken to combat this menace we are in danger of losing one of our greatest natural assets. I submit therefore, Mr. Speaker, that this affects not only the actual area involved but the entire Dominion of Canada. It has been estimated that the western farmer has had his purchasing power reduced to the amount of $450,000,000 a year since 1929. This undoubtedly has had a disastrous effect upon the industrial areas of eastern Canada. I feel, as has been already suggested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), that these conditions constitute a national menace. Were an epidemic or a flood or a forest fire to break out in any part of Canada, the government would promptly rush assistance to the district affected. I contend that an equally serious calamity has occurred and that definite steps must be taken at once.
The first step which I think should be taken, and indeed must be taken, is that the people within that area shall be guaranteed at least food, clothing, shelter, fuel and the necessary medical services. It is hardly necessary to stress this point. In a country which produces wealth to the extent that Canada does, there is no need for any person, or any group of persons, to suffer privation. But may I say this cannot be done if provincial relief grants are to be cut, as has been announced in the press, on April next. There can be no money in western Canada until after the next crop, if there is a crop. Most of the provinces are close to bankruptcy; they have been unable to collect their taxes, and a reduction in relief grants could have only one result, namely, a lower standard of living for our hard pressed people in the drought area.

The second step which I would suggest is a rehabilitation program similar in some respects to that outlined by the minister. The speech from the throne this session contains this sentence:
A comprehensive program to meet the serious conditions created by widespread and intense drought in western Canada was adopted during the summer months.
Without being unduly critical, may I say that while such a program may have been adopted, no material evidences of it were at all apparent in the large part of southern Saskatchewan which I covered.
The constituency from which I come borders on the international boundary, so I have had an excellent opportunity of studying the work being carried on by the United States government in what is commonly called their "dust bowl." In an area slightly smaller than our drought area the United States is spending $500,000,000 over a period of ten years. This means $50,000,000 a year. Compare this with the situation in Canada, where we have spent $850,000 in two years in rehabilitating the drought area. In other words, we are spending less than one per cent of the amount being spent by the United States government in the same period in a slightly smaller area, admitting, of course, that the United States area is much more densely populated.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that if rehabilitation is to be anything more than a mere gesture, we must be prepared to spend at least $5,000,000 per year over a ten-year period in order to produce any serious effect in retarding the ravages of the present drought and to take the necessary measures to meet a recurring drought. There may be some dismay experienced at a figure of $5,000,000 per year. The other evening the right hon. leader of the opposition reminded the house that there is a limitation upon the money which may be expended, having relation to the benefits to be derived therefrom, and to this the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) nodded his assent. May I point out that $5,000,000 is not anywhere near the point of limitation.
No one suggested that it was.

I am not suggesting that; I am merely saying, with reference to the figure I am citing, that it is nowhere near the point of limitation. In the first place, this area constitutes the granary of the world. It would cost a great deal more than $5,000,000 if we were to lose some of the finest wheat growing land in Canada or if we had to

Farm Rehabilitation-Mr. Douglas
transport and resettle the people now living in the area. May I point out also that under an appropriate rehabilitation scheme whereby wages would be paid for services rendered, this $5,000,000 would not be expended entirely on rehabilitation; it would relieve us of the necessity of paying relief in some instances, and thereby a saving would be effected.
Let us examine, therefore, whether there is any hope of such an expenditure being warranted. It is often said that no matter what you do you cannot change the climate. That is granted, but there are things we can do. I have before me reports on a number of surveys that have been made by engineers, some under the auspices of the Canadian Conservation Institute and others under the direction of Secretary Wallace of the United States Department of Agriculture. Most of these reports agree on one or two cardinal points. The first is that the great tragedy of the drought was due to the fact that we were not prepared for it. The second point on which they agree is that the reason for most of the suffering occasioned by drought, was not merely the lack of crop but the lack of the necessary water to sustain stock, water gardens and carry on the ordinary routine of life. In short, the real tragedy was that the farmer was no longer able to supply his own table and feed his family. Had the average farmer been able to keep his cattle, hogs, chickens, horses and so on; had he been able to irrigate even a small garden, the loss of crops would not have occasioned anything like the suffering which has come to the people in the drought areas during the past six years. Most engineers are agreed that while we cannot change the drought cycle, nevertheless we can prepare for the contingency of drought. Some authorities contend that the drought cycle ended in 1936, which may or may not be true. If the present drought cycle is broken-and we hope it is-then not only must we rehabilitate the soil from the ravages of the drought that has taken place, we must also take measures against future contingencies.
Whether we like it or not, Mr. Speaker, drought will continue to be a recurring problem. The measures to which we may resort have been dealt with already to some extent by the Minister of Agriculture, but I wish to group them into three classifications. In the first class are those measures necessary for replacing fibre in the soil. In the second class is the conservation of water, in order to keep

stock alive. In the third class are steps to prevent, as far as possible, evaporation of moisture, which is so great a factor in soil drifting.
With reference to the first group, the replacement of fibre in the soil, I quote from the report of the Canadian Conservation Institute, which makes the following suggestions: First, soil drifting can be largely prevented; second, strip farming is at least effective temporarily until other factors are adjusted; third, cover crops help and, fourth, fibre can be returned to the soil by growing forage crops.
Then it is no longer wheat producing land.

That will be true of some of the areas, and I shall be more specific about that in a moment. There are areas which never should have been opened up for the production of wheat, principally the highlands, which are dotted here and there with lowlands which can be used for wheat production. Not only that, but farmers have been in the habit of leaving a large part of their farms in summer fallow every third year. Now they have come to the point where, if they can afford to do so, instead of leaving part of their farms in summer fallow, they put in some cover crop in order to put fibre back into the soil. In North Dakota I came across a number of farmers whose soil had been tested. The nitrate qualities were still in the soil; the difficulty was that the soil had been reduced to a powder by the constant erosion of the wind with the result that the soil lacked fibre. The government of the United States, under the A.A.A. program, gave these farmers crested wheat grass seed free of charge and paid them $7 an acre to put it in. They did so, and the results were twofold. In the first place, the farmer was no longer dependent upon relief in any shape or form; he had enough to buy feed for his horses and was able to keep his machinery in a state of repair. Now I should like to say a word1 with regard to water conservation. As I have suggested already, during the drought the main difficulty was that it caught us unprepared. The impounding of water in small bodies would make it possible for a farmer in the drought area at least to keep himself and his stock. The other evening someone said you could not impound water if it was not there, and unfortunately in many districts that is only too true. But in many districts there is water which is not being impounded. In the spring of 1934 I stood at a point twelve miles north of the town of Trossachs and watched many tons of water pouring down into a gully. When I came back three months later, it was a desert where one could not even pasture cattle. Some steps should be taken in such places to catch the freshets in the spring by means of small dams built to hold water so that the horses might be kept alive. This might be done in three ways. First of all, individual dug-outs might be built on the farms. The Minister of Agriculture has said that, despite the fact that the government has been offering $76 for the building of dug-outs, very few of them have been built. The explanation is simple. First of all, it costs $150 to dig a dug-out to the specifications set down by the department, and this means that the farmer must be able to put up the other $75. But that is not the most serious handicap; the real handicap is that the farmer must have the necessary scrapers and these he has to borrow from the municipality. But when he borrows them

and has only his son or a hired man to help him, it takes several weeks to dig the dug-out, and while they are digging it, other farmers in the community have not the use of the scraper. Unless there can be some way of paying the farmers so much per day or supplying feed for their horses and putting in sufficient machinery to enable them to work in groups, no progress will be made. A group of men could dig a dug-out in less than a week, whereas the individual farmer without any assistance will work the entire summer at it. In Manitoba, I understand, the provincial government has put out digging machines with the result that an entire dug-out is made in a day. That is not done in the part of the country I come from, and there is need of it. If every farmer had in his backyard an individual dug-out according to the specifications set by the department, he could see his way through the summer and would be able to keep his stock alive.
Will the dug-outs hold water?

Yes, they will. I had thought the water would seep away, but this has not happened. The ground is so hard that it retains the water. This fall I visited dugouts made a year ago and it did not seem possible that animals had been drinking from them at all.
Does the water not get very foul?

Yes; it would not be fit for human consumption, but it is excellent for stock. Another method would be to build small dams in some places. Farmers who have good horses and can buy feed should be able to build these dams very successfully, but a great many of the farmers are not in a position to do this. Again, there is the possibility of putting gangs of men to work. Here I would refer to the United States, though of course I do not suggest that we should follow them slavishly. In North Dakota and Montana I found groups of men working. A farmer working by himself received $4.80 a day, and a man with a team of horses received $8.80.
That was before the election.

He was allowed only ten day's work. The elections may have had something to do with it, but I know the results were beneficial. It gave the people purchasing power and it gave them supplies of water for their cattle. Another thing that can be done has already been mentioned, and that is the building of municipal dams.

Once the problem of storing water has been settled, the next question to be considered is the possibility of retaining the moisture and of preventing evaporation. This could be accomplished by planting shrubs and trees and keeping summer fallow from lying bare by having coverage growing on it.
I suggest that the attitude taken by the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon will be something of an inspiration and encouragement to the people of the drought area. May I suggest to the government that the spending of less than an average of half a million dollars over a period of two years does not begin to touch the problem. It seems to me that in the past two years the government have been penny-wise and pound-foolish, in connection with this scheme. We have spent less than one per cent of what our neighbours to the south have spent in dealing with a similar problem. Five million dollars a year may look like a lot of money, but I submit that the returns warrant it, especially when we remember that in last year's budget we set aside $140,000,000 to meet interest on funded debt, and this year it will be $138,000,000. What has that to do with the question?

The point I desire to make beyond all question is that parliament, in setting up an advisory rehabilitation committee as distinct from a local committee, differentiated a national concern from a domestic concern; a matter in which all the taxpayers of the country are interested from one in which those who are upon the soil in the localities in question are interested; those who are concerned with their investments from those who have borrowed, and all this is dealt with in this statute by imposing a limitation upon the appointments. That advisory committee, serving without pay, was selected with these limitations, so that there could not be any possible chance of any racket with respect to it, or any favouritism. kept thoroughly informed and in - a position to make such representations as might be thought desirable to ensure the national nature of the undertaking.

Then it goes on to recite where those men may be chosen from. Then the act continues:
4.	The committee shall consider and advise the minister as to the best methods to be adopted to secure the rehabilitation of the drought and soil drifting areas in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta and to develop and promote within those areas systems of farm practice, tree culture and water supply that will afford greater economic security and to make such representations thereon to the minister as the committee may deem expedient.
5.	No member of the committee shall receive any payment or emolument for his services, but he shall be repaid all actual reasonable travelling or other expenses in connection with the work of the committee.
6.	The minister may appoint such temporary technical, professional and other officers and employees as he may deem necessary and expedient for carrying out the provisions of this act and the salaries and expenses of such officers shall be fixed by the governor in council.

First of all, I want to express my regret for the fact that the legislation passed by the former government has been disallowed by the privy council. I hope the minister will use his most vigorous efforts to continue the line of activity of the last government to do something for labour. The previous government never received the credit they should have received for the honest efforts they made to help workmen throughout the country. They endeavoured to see that there was no violation of the minimum wage law, that the workers should work only for a reasonable week and that the hours of labour per day should be limited. When the legislation proposed by the late government was going through the house, the draft conventions and recommendations of the international labour conferences from 1919 to 1934 were referred to. I believe that at that time the then member for Kenora-Rainy River, who had previously been the Minister of Labour, the Hon. Mr. Heenan, supported the efforts of the government to relieve the disabilities under which workmen are now labouring. Article I of draft convention number 26 reads:
Each member of the international labour organization which ratifies this convention undertakes to create or maintain machinery whereby minimum rates of wages can be fixed

for workers employed in certain of the trades or parts of trades (and in particular in home working trades) in which no arrangements exist for the effective regulation of wages by collective agreement or other-wise and wages are exceptionally low.
It is about time that we had some law in Canada to control the rates as to minimum wages. Where there is no control over wages, we have sweat shop conditions, and there is too much of that in this country. For years the International Labour Union has endeavoured to induce all governments to adopt minimum wage laws. I am one of those who like to support the efforts of this union and the unions associated with it in Canada to ensure better conditions for the working man in the way of better wages and treatment. I am not one of those who condemn industry. My observations have been that industry generally treats the labouring man fairly. There is the odd industrialist who brings censure on industry generally. It was to take care of that odd man who does not treat labour properly that these draft conventions respecting minimum wages, hours of labour and the weekly day of rest were adopted. The minister, I am convinced, has at heart the best interests of the workers of this country, and I sincerely hope that he will achieve something along these lines. We read almost daily of men and women working an outrageous number of hours per week, apparently because the federal government has not sufficient authority, as I am convinced it should have, to enforce its will in this regard in the various provinces.
The time is past when one province or another-and I have no particular province in mind at the moment-should permit conditions to prevail in factories, which conditions another province would not tolerate for one minute. I am convinced the time has come- and I am sorry the privy council did not see it in that way-when this parliament should endeavour to bring about uniform conditions in labour from one end of Canada to the other. Uniform conditions in labour throughout Canada would work against the practice of employers in one province moving their whole plant to another province where labour restrictions are not as severe. I could name offhand a number, and I could easily obtain a list of perhaps fifty factories that in the last few years have moved from the city of Toronto to another province than Ontario, because in Toronto so far as possible industrialists are induced by compulsion, public opinion, and perhaps by the local government, which I believe does endeavour to carry out the majority will of the operators in this regard, to provide decent working conditions.

What is the result to-day? I have no hesitation in saying that it was one of the greatest social acts enacted by a British parliament. I appreciate the fact that the work is being done from Montreal and I have no particular criticism of the officer, but it has been brought to my attention at different times that there is a desire to have an officer appointed for the maritime provinces, to be located there, and I suggest that the most suitable place would be somewhere in New Brunswick, possibly Saint John.
Other suitable places have been suggested.

I may say for the information of the hon. member for St. John-Albert that there was a fair wage officer at Halifax and he was removed by the late administration. Mr. Quirk comes from Halifax and has always been most satisfactory in every respect. I am only too pleased to be able to make that statement. I do think that the minister, together with his deputy and his assistants, might take into consideration the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. John-Albert, but I must add that I cannot endorse the idea that an officer should be moved from Halifax and the new appointee be located in Saint John.
Are there any employees working on government projects or in government offices more than eight hours a day or six days a week? I have been informed that there are individuals who do.

If there are any complaints of that kind I shall be glad to have them brought to my attention, and if they fall within the Fair Wage Act it is the duty of the Department of Labour to see that the matter is rectified. It may be that certain projects are excepted from the operation of the Fair Wage Act. The act itself provides for such exception by order in council, but from the information given by my hon. friend I am not able to say whether the eight hour day is being exceeded in any particular project.

The complaint made to me has reference to firemen working in

the barracks in the city of Calgary. I was informed that they were working seven days a week and sometimes fen hours a day.
I shall be glad to look into the matter.
Are there more than two fair wage officers in Canada?
There are four in all.
Where are they located?
One in Vancouver, one in Toronto, one in Ottawa and one in Montreal.
Has any section of the dominion complained that it has not received proper attention from these officers?

There have been suggestions from time to time that there should be a fair wage officer resident in the maritime provinces. The matter referred to a moment ago by the hon. member for St. John-Albert has received the attention of the department, and we realize that there are some reasons- particularly the question of easy access in cases of dispute-which seem to recommend the appointment of a fair wage officer in the maritime provinces. On the other hand, we have not yet been convinced that the eastern representative is not able to work satisfactorily. It will be remembered that provision is now being made for the appointment of four junior conciliation officers, and with that addition to the staff it may be possible to meet the situation which we have been discussing.
Under the act for the organization and coordination of employment services, what is the amount of the subventions paid to the various provinces?
I take it the hon. member wants to have the apportionment of the 8150,000 among the various provinces?
Yes.

The minister speaks of four special officers who are practically undersecretaries in his department, and I gather from what he has said that perhaps one of these might be assigned to the maritimes. Am I correct?
I think that might meet the situation.

I think the policy shall be to appoint as fair wage officer a person who is in contact with and has the viewpoint of the interests of the various sections of Canada and knows the industry in which labour is employed. Mr. Martin held that position at Halifax and his services were dispensed IMr. I.anderyou.]
with by the late administration. The person appointed should be one who has knowledge of local conditions in the maritime provinces, if there is to be one for the three provinces, and is in sympathy with the industries there and with labour generally. When these juniors to be appointed have become acquainted with local conditions it might be wise-I do not say it would-to consider assigning them to these various duties, in order to keep down the expenditure of the department. But I concur in the view of the hon. member for St. John-Albert that at least a maritime man should be appointed who knows conditions there; that was the policy of the administration prior to 1930- and I suggest to the minister the viewpoint which has been expressed by the hon. member for St. John-Albert, and in which I believe my colleague the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), who I am sorry is not in his seat at the moment, would concur. I should be pleased to confer at any time with the minister and my colleague and any other hon. member from the maritime provinces to present our views and receive those of the minister.
